newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish NFI 11 mulls sale of cement firm Rejowiec.
newsitem.headline: Polish NFI 11 mulls sale of cement firm Rejowiec.

text.p: Polish National Investment Fund (NFI) No. 11, fresh from gaining $10 million from selling shares in the Wierzbica SA cement firm, is mulling selling another firm from the sector, the fund's spokesman said.

Maciej Tekielski told Reuters the fund, one of 15 such institutions set up under the mass privatisation scheme, was considering calling a tender for its 33 percent stake in Rejowiec SA cement maker, located in eastern Poland.
"The fund is considering whether to call a tender (for Rejowiec)," Tekielski said. Some firms have already shown interest in the purchase, he added without elaborating.

In November France's Lafarge LAFP.WA bought 60 percent in Wierzbica -- a 33 percent held by the NFI No. 11 and 27 percent from other 14 funds in scheme. The 14 funds gained a total of $20 million from the sale, Tekielski said.
Upon the sale last November PAP news agency said Wierzbica netted 200,000 zlotys in 1995 on 68.4 million zlotys in sales.
Tekielski said Rejowiec netted 0.6 million zlotys over 1996's first nine months on sales of 46.5 million zlotys.
Under the NFI mass privatisation scheme shares in some 500 firms are allocated to 15 NFIs run by foreign and domestic management firms.

The 26 million Poles who bought a participation unit in the scheme will be entitled to exchange it for 15 shares, one in each fund, which are expected to start trade on the Warsaw bourse in the first half of this year.
Each fund controls 33 percent of more than 30 firms and 1.9 percent in each of the rest.

Tekielski also said two of its other firms, mining equipment maker Fasing SA and the PZZ Boleslawiec SA grain mill, had sent issue prospectuses to the Securities Commission (KPW) to enter the fledgling over-the-counter market.

He said the funds from the Wierzbica sale would go to restructuring some of its firms, while some would go to the creation of a growth fund, to which the fund had already put one to two percent of its assets.
"We hope that by the end of 1999 we will have close to 50 percent of our assets in the growth fund (which) would be comparable to a closed-end investment fund," Tekielski said.
